Surprisingly compelling Big Brother simulator that follows in the same vein of games like "Papers, Please" and "Beholder." Orwell is a GUI point and click choose your own text-based adventure.  Minimal audio limited to ambiance, punctuated occasionally by tension-inducing background music.  Intriguing story surrounding the security vs. privacy debate with real world implications.

Recommendation:  Get it during a sale; definitely worth playing!

PROS:
+ Relevant and topical story
+ Interface is easy to learn and feels natural
+ Plausible system mechanics aids in the suspension of disbelief
+ NPCs have interesting personalities
+ Difficulty increases at the end to maintain interest
+ Multiple endings with satisfying results; good replayability

CONS:
+ Minor text/grammar errors in a text-based game are bad, avoidable through QA/QC
+ Game is a bit short, can be beaten in just a few hours - which is why I recommend only getting it on sale
+ Listening in on phone calls looks/plays exactly like reading a text message conversation; i.e. boring
+ Can feel railroad-y, especially at the very beginning tutorial part

Simply put, Orwell condenses all of the moral arguments surrounding a surveilance state to a "let's see you do it."

You are responsible for guiding a PRISM-like system in a quest to unravel violent events surrounding a group opposed to the intrusions upon society.  Somewhat true to life, your superiors act on what information you condense down to them - they don't actually read everything (that's 'your job').  You get to eavesdrop, sift through a computer's hard drive, peruse the private accounts of citizens... all in a quest to 'do the right thing.'

The ethical dilemma is appropriate.  There is a very real threat to the game's citizens.  Yet, you can easily pass along information out of its proper context and paint a picture that doesn't exist from within the ocean-spray of people's activity on the internet.  Even very early into the game, you find yourself ignoring far more text than you are reading as the scope of the investigation expands and you find yourself 'scope locked' to the auto-tag system.

There is some replayability, as well.  Events are influenced by what information you pass along, as well as how you react to some real-time scenarios.

This is where it becomes interesting - your superior isn't entirely sure of everything you are seeing.  You can see that someone is planning a hack in real time... and just ... let it happen.  Or, you can see that a person suspects they are being monitored, and pass along tactical information that could be disinformation.  This is partially where the ethical context of the game comes into play, as the events can unfold in many different ways depending upon how you, as an individual, wish them to.  Don't like a person?  Try to land them in jail.  Like a character?  Try to shield them from the investigation ... or guide the investigation to them in order to justify unleashing the full resources of Orwell on their private life.

Perhaps the forest amid all the trees, however, is that the entire conflict of, at least, the first story arc would not exist were it not for the very system used to defend against it.

In all, it's a great exploration of the ethics of our evolving soviety.  Highly recommended for its philosophical exploration, alone.

Excellent game, thoroughly enjoyed it.  Basically everything would be a spoiler so I'm not going to mention anything game specific, but it plays out like a text-based Telltale game.  Also meta, but not in an obnoxious way - I appreciate that.

As for critiques, it was very irritating to discover information prior to being allowed to select, even when you *know* it is pertinent to the investigation. It felt like too much handholding (with pre-highlighted phrases), and too many bottlenecks stopping me from filling out my investigation at my own pace.  AND LET PLAYERS ZOOM OUT ON THE CONNECTIONS/CONTACTS MAP! It was infuriating scrolling around.  Also, from an intelligence standpoint, the paths to other persons in the contact networks should be labelled with their relationship (Brother, Sister, Girlfriend, etc.) and updated as you discover more information just like everything else. 

Cosmetic Bug: The player can choose which primary profile picture they associate with each person, which changes that picture in all subsequent documents or interactions (calls, texts), but during one scripted cutscene it defaulted to what would probably have been the newest picture I had discovered (Nina in this case) when I had purposely switched to a prior picture. No one would normally notice, but it is still a jarring bug because they were very different pictures and it didn't make logical sense with the way I was building the narrrative for Orwell.
